blocks.content: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India. It regulates the country's monetary system and manages the currency and credit system of the economy. It plays a vital role in maintaining financial stability and controlling inflation.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Reserve Bank of India was established on April 1, 1935, based on the recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission.
RBI was nationalised on January 1, 1949, transforming it into a fully state-owned central banking institution.
It acts as the sole issuer of bank notes in India, excluding one-rupee notes and coins which are issued by the Ministry of Finance.
RBI regulates monetary policy using quantitative instruments (Repo, CRR, SLR) and qualitative instruments (Moral Suasion, Margin Requirements).
It acts as the banker to the government, banker's bank, and custodian of India's foreign exchange reserves under FEMA 1999.

blocks.content: • It was established under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
• The headquarters of RBI is located in Mumbai.
• To regulate the issue of banknotes.
• To maintain monetary stability in the country.
• To operate the currency and credit system.
The Reserve Bank of India was established on April 1, 1935, in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.

cells: RBI issues currency notes except one-rupee note.
RBI manages accounts of central and state governments.

blocks.content: • Repo Rate – Rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks.
• Reverse Repo Rate – Rate at which RBI borrows money from banks.
• Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) – Percentage of deposits banks must keep with RBI.
• Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) – Percentage of deposits banks must maintain in liquid assets.

blocks.content: • Open Market Operations – Buying and selling government securities.
• Central Board of Directors – Governing body.

items: Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended the setup of RBI; Sir Osborne Smith was its first Governor and C.D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor.
One-rupee notes carry the signature of the Finance Secretary, whereas other currency notes bear the RBI Governor's signature.
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is maintained in liquid cash with the RBI, whereas Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is maintained by commercial banks with themselves in approved securities or cash.
